title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1): Caching
summary: Defines HTTP caches and the header fields that control cache behavior or mark responses as cacheable. It was part of the revision of HTTP/1.1 that replaced RFC 2616. It was later replaced by RFC 9111.

plainLanguage.summary: A cache is like keeping a copy of a library book on your desk so you do not have to walk to the library each time. This explains the rules for when the copy is still good. A newer version has replaced it.

questions: when can a response be cached
when is a cached response fresh
subtitle: Rules for storing and reusing HTTP responses to improve performance.

tldr.problem: Fetching the same web resource repeatedly from the origin server wastes bandwidth and increases latency. Caches need standard rules for when they can safely reuse a stored response instead of asking the origin again.
tldr.mechanism: Caches use header fields like Cache-Control, Expires, and ETag to decide when a stored response is fresh (reusable without validation) or stale (needing revalidation from the origin). The Vary header handles cases where different representations exist for the same URI.
tldr.outcome: Caching is a critical performance optimization for the web. RFC 7234 obsoleted RFC 2616 and was itself replaced by RFC 9111 with clarifications and updates for modern HTTP.

facts.label: Default Heuristic Freshness
facts.value: Up to 10% of time since Last-Modified

today: RFC 7234 defines HTTP/1.1 caching and was part of the HTTP/1.1 specification update that obsoleted RFC 2616. It was later replaced by RFC 9111, which provides updates and clarifications for modern web caching. Caching remains essential to web performance and is widely implemented in browsers, CDNs, and intermediary proxies.

sections.title: What Is HTTP Caching?
sections.content:
An HTTP cache is a local store of HTTP responses and the system that controls what gets stored, retrieved, and deleted. A cache stores cacheable responses to reduce response time and network bandwidth on future equivalent requests. Both clients and servers may employ caches. A shared cache serves multiple users (usually at an intermediary such as a proxy or CDN), while a private cache is dedicated to a single user (typically in a browser).

The goal of caching is to improve performance by reusing prior responses. A stored response is fresh if its age has not yet exceeded its freshness lifetime; it can be reused without validation. A stale response has exceeded its freshness lifetime. Stale responses might still be reusable if they can be freshened through validation or if the origin is unavailable.
sections.plainLanguage: A cache keeps copies of web pages. Fresh copies are still good and you can use them right away. Stale copies might need a quick check with the server before you show them, or you can use them if the server is down.

sections.title: What Gets Stored in a Cache?
sections.content:
A cache MUST NOT store a response unless all of these conditions are met: the request method is understood and cacheable, the response status code is understood, the "no-store" directive is absent from both request and response, the "private" directive does not appear (if it is a shared cache), and the Authorization header is absent unless the response explicitly allows caching. Additionally, the response must either contain explicit expiration time (via Expires or max-age), a status code that is cacheable by default (like 200, 203, 204, 206, 300, 301, 404, 405, 410, 414, or 501), or a "public" directive.

Caches can also store responses to incomplete range requests, combining multiple partial responses into a single stored entry if they share the same validator. Responses to authenticated requests (with Authorization) may be stored only if the response includes caching directives like must-revalidate, public, or s-maxage.
sections.plainLanguage: A cache only saves pages that are allowed to be saved. If the server says "do not store this" or says "only store if it is marked public," the cache obeys.

sections.title: Freshness and Validation
sections.content:
A response's freshness lifetime is how long it can be reused without checking with the server. An origin server provides explicit expiration times using the Expires header (an absolute time) or the max-age directive (a duration in seconds). If no explicit expiration is given, a cache may assign a heuristic freshness lifetime using algorithms based on header fields like Last-Modified, but only for responses with cacheable status codes and no explicit expiration.

A response's age is how long it has existed since being generated or validated by the origin. The freshness check is simple: if age has not exceeded freshness_lifetime, the response is fresh. When a cached response is not fresh but a stored entry exists, the cache can send a conditional request using validators like ETag or Last-Modified to check whether the stored response is still valid. If the origin responds with 304 (Not Modified), the cache freshens its stored response and reuses it. Otherwise, the cache replaces the stale entry with the new response.
sections.plainLanguage: Every cached page has an expiration date. After that date, the page is stale. But you can ask the server "is your copy newer than mine?" and if it says no, your copy is still good.

sections.title: Cache Control Directives
sections.content:
The Cache-Control header carries directives for both requests and responses. Request directives include max-age (accept fresh responses up to this age), min-fresh (minimum freshness required), and no-cache (require validation). Response directives include public (can be cached by shared caches even with Authorization), private (only for private caches), max-age (freshness lifetime), s-maxage (freshness lifetime for shared caches only), must-revalidate (never serve stale without validation), proxy-revalidate (for shared caches), and no-cache (requires validation before reuse even if fresh).

The Expires header specifies an absolute expiration time as an HTTP-date. If both Expires and max-age are present, max-age takes precedence. The Pragma header exists for backward compatibility and should not be used for new content; caches should follow Cache-Control instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Cache-Control tells the cache what to do. "max-age=3600" means "keep for one hour." "must-revalidate" means "always ask before using an old copy." "public" means "okay to share with other users."

sections.title: Cache Keys and Content Negotiation
sections.content: The primary cache key consists of the request method and target URI. Multiple responses may be stored for the same URI if the server uses content negotiation (serving different representations based on request headers like Accept, Accept-Language, or Accept-Encoding). The Vary header indicates which request header fields select among multiple representations. When a cache receives a request for a URI with a Vary header, it must match all the selecting header fields between the stored response's original request and the new request. If the headers do not match, the cache cannot use that stored response and must contact the origin.
sections.plainLanguage: A cache key is usually just the web address. But if the server says "I have different versions in different languages," the cache must remember which language each copy is for and pick the right one.

sections.title: Validation, Stale Responses, and Warnings
sections.content:
When a stale response exists and the origin server is available, the cache should validate it using conditional requests (If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since, If-Range). The origin responds with 304 (Not Modified) to indicate the stored response is valid, allowing the cache to freshen and reuse it. A 200 or other full response means the stale entry is replaced.

In some cases, such as when the origin is disconnected or when the client explicitly allows it with max-stale, a cache MAY serve a stale response. When doing so, it SHOULD add a Warning header field to alert the client that the response is stale. Warning code 110 indicates "Response is Stale", while code 112 indicates "Disconnected Operation".

Unsafe methods (POST, PUT, DELETE) must be written through to the origin server and cannot be answered from a cache. Safe methods (GET, HEAD) may invalidate existing cache entries based on cache-control directives.
sections.plainLanguage: If a copy gets too old, the cache can ask "is yours newer?" If the server says no, the old copy is good. If the server is down but you really need a page, you can show the stale copy with a warning label.
